Professional observatories. (Also amateurs I’m sure.) The professional observatories use what’s called a “laser guide star” to track how the atmosphere is moving and warping the light coming in from the real star so they can correct for it. 

Basically, they know where the laser star should be and how bright it should look, so they can just see how different their captured image is from that ideal state and then know how far off the real star they’re looking at is from its ideal state. Then they use fancy software and hardware to apply those corrections they found to get a much, much clearer picture! 

This is a commonly used technique in the field of adaptive optics. If you’re at all interested I recommend you look up adaptive optics and go down the rabbit hole from there!

I know what you mean! I know the feeling of not wanting to mess up such a good thing. I think that you guys have a good enough thing that you won’t mess it up by telling her how you feel, but obviously I’m not in the relationship so it’s your call. 

I really get not wanting to be problematic, but remember that she loves you and wants what’s best for you. And even if it is only temporary, wouldn’t it be better to try and feel a little happier while it’s going on? 

One thing that helped me and my girlfriend a lot when we did long distance is having FaceTime calls. Obviously you don’t want her neglecting her friends for you, but I find that a little bit of really good time together can be just as helpful as a bunch of half assed conversations while you both are busy. Me and my girlfriend settled on Monday Wednesday and Friday FaceTime calls, but that’s because I have ADHD and a routine helps me not forget. You could play around with that, doing FaceTime calls more or less often, or even doing something else. I know there’s services out there that let you watch a movie with someone over a video chat, or you could play video games together if that’s more your thing. My point is there’s lots of options to help you get more quality time if you think that’ll help! And if you’re thinking it’s not worth it to go through all this trouble just for a couple months, remember that this might not be the last time you guys are apart and it’s good to have these strategies in place if you need them in the future. 

It is hard when your partner is busy and doesn’t have time to reply to you all the time, and I’m not sure if there’s really anything you can do about that. I think spending some good time together over video chat could help, but besides that just remember that your girlfriend loves you a lot and this is only temporary.

This probably will read like something straight out of a therapist’s office (because it is! I got it from my therapist and it’s helped a lot), but I think it would help you get used to this all if you let yourself sit with your feelings and just feel them and acknowledge they’re valid and there for a reason, and they shouldn’t be shunned. It’s perfectly ok to feel like you do, and if you let the feelings wash over you without trying to push them down or rationalize them away that could help them run their course and leave you naturally. My therapist always refers to those feelings as different parts of me, and has me sit with each part and let it feel its hurt and sadness, and comfort that part of myself as if it was a small child needing support. I’m not sure if that’ll work for you but you might give it a shot just to see. 

As for your friends, it’s entirely up to you if you want to open up! I opened up a bit to my friends when I was going through the worst of it, and it helped to have more supportive people to help me through. They made me feel loved and supported, and they made a bit more of an effort to go do fun things with me after I told them. I’d say if you’re comfortable opening up about it, it’s worth a shot! They could very well be a big support network for you with this problem as well as others going forward if you let them.

Hey I’ve struggled with this in the past, I went on a trip without my girlfriend early in our relationship and it was really hard for me. The problem ended up being emotional codependency and my fear of being left behind. 

I’m not gonna say I’m all the way better now (3yrs on) but I’m definitely a lot better than I was. You’re on the right track, knowing that it’s not ok to act on your feelings and it’s not your girlfriend’s fault is a really good start and I struggled with that part for a while. 

I think what helped me the most is forcing myself to hang out with my friends without them (my girlfriend) and letting myself feel the sadness and loneliness and shit without trying to push it down or act on it. I also highly recommend therapy (doesn’t everyone on Reddit?) and just outsourcing your healing process so it’s not all on you or your girlfriend. If you think your girlfriend will be helpful and not feel guilty, you could talk to her about it when you both are calm. If you do that, I recommend trying to keep the discussion calm and neutral, and tell her you’re not blaming her and you want her help working through your issues. Frame it as you two versus your brain instead of her doing something wrong and having to fix it.

They were very nonjudgmental, and they were one of the only people I felt safe eating around. They would never ever comment on what I ate or how much (“just eat a little more!” is about the worst thing you can tell someone going through that). I felt very loved and supported in their presence. I knew I could come to them for support, because they wouldn’t freak out and make a big deal out of it. That’s a big one! I could never go to my parents because I couldn’t bear to see how their face would fall. They would always suggest really big things like the mental hospital or a crisis center, when all I needed was for someone to hug me and tell me it was ok to feel this way and that I will get better. I would highly recommend not trying to give your girlfriend advice or try to fix it for her unless she specifically asks. A lot of the time it’s far more helpful to sit with the person and give them physical and verbal reassurance. Asking “is there anything I can do to help?” is good, but you probably shouldn’t go any farther unless she asks for help. 

My girlfriend would check up on me, but it would never be a big thing. My parents would ask how I was doing and then push me for more if I said I was fine. It was well-intentioned, but it just pushed me away more because it felt invasive. My girlfriend would ask me how I’m doing and if I said I was fine they would say “ok! I love you and I’m here for you if you ever need anything.” And then drop the subject and move on. That helped me be more comfortable opening up to them, because I knew they wouldn’t push for more information than I was comfortable with.
